slides.title: Stage-1 Calibration: Test Procedure and Robot Program
slides.subtitle: Running the capture session and what the robot program must do
slides.notes: This is the second of two decks on the stage-1 calibration captures. The first covers procurement and the mechanical build. This one covers the session: setup in the robot cell, the pose plan, the robot program's job, how poses are recorded, and the checks. It summarizes sections 2 to 11 of the stage-1 capture procedure in docs/procedures.

slides.title: The session produces data plus an exact table of poses

stats.label: robot time with fixture changes and checks
accuracy target at 500 mm, scaling with distance

slides.message: If the pose table is wrong, the calibration is wrong.
slides.body: Every capture file must be matched to the target that was in view and to exactly where the robot put it. Most of the procedure is about getting that table right.
slides.notes: The output of a session is a folder of sensor capture files, one group per robot pose, and a manifest that records for every file which target was in view and exactly where the robot had placed it. The software compares what the sensor measured with the known geometry of the target at that known pose. Any error in the table goes straight into the correction map, so most of the procedure's steps exist to make the table trustworthy. The accuracy target is 0.1 mm at 500 mm, scaling with distance; the robot's own absolute accuracy of 0.1 mm is of the same size, which is why the robot pose must be the reported one, not the commanded one.

slides.title: The session at a glance

steps.head: Prepare
steps.text: Warm up the sensor 30 min; fix exposure, gain and SGM parameters

steps.head: Mount spheres
steps.text: Doweled adapter and stem; find each sphere's TCP in the nest

steps.head: Board frame
steps.text: Runout check; set the tool frame on the front face

steps.head: Locate sensor
steps.text: Four sphere captures give a rough sensor position

steps.head: Plan poses
steps.text: The plan tool writes 186 poses and a picture

steps.head: Capture
steps.text: Sphere A, then sphere B, then the board

steps.head: Manifest
steps.text: Pose log and files become the manifest

steps.head: Check
steps.text: Quick check before the robot and fixtures are put away

slides.notes: These are the eight stages of a session, in order; sections 2 to 8 of the procedure correspond to them. Steps 1 to 4 are setup and happen once per session. Step 5 runs the plan tool, which needs the rough sensor position from step 4. Step 6 is the long robot run. Steps 7 and 8 run software on the capture computer or the engineer's laptop, and step 8 should happen while everything is still set up, so a flagged pose can be captured again at once.

slides.title: Preparation before the first session

columns.head: Robot
points: Check the documented absolute accuracy: 0.1 mm or better
Weigh each fixture; enter its tool load data
Write the robot program; note where it writes pose_log.csv
Dry-run every pose at reduced speed
Safety review of the new program

columns.head: Sensor and computers
points: Capture software set for the robot's trigger and the file names
Exposure, gain and SGM parameters set and recorded: smoothing filters off, installation patch size
10 GB free per 1,000 frames
Calibration software installed and self-tested

columns.head: Cell
points: Layout study: the 300 to 1,100 mm volume inside the robot's reach
Table drilled and tapped for the nest and the run-out plate
Robot base frame identified and recorded

slides.message: The fixtures and tools themselves are in the procurement and build deck, and in section 1 of the procedure.
slides.notes: This is section 1f of the procedure: everything to prepare before the first session, beyond the fixtures and tools. The robot's absolute accuracy is taken from its documented specification. Tool load data matters because an absolute-accuracy robot compensates for load, so a wrong mass or center of gravity shifts every pose. The capture trigger goes through the capture computer's existing communication software, so the robot program only needs to call it. The SGM parameters are set the way installations use them except that smoothing filters are off, so the calibration sees the sensor's raw matching. The layout study comes first, because it fixes where the sensor mount goes.

slides.title: The three-ball nest finds each sphere's center

steps.text: Enter a rough TCP from caliper measurements, and the fixture's tool load data
Run the robot's multi-orientation TCP routine with at least six seatings: stem up, tilted 40 degrees four ways, one twisted
Accept only a routine error of 0.1 mm or less
Re-seat at a very different wrist angle: positions agree within 0.1 mm

slides.notes: The robot cannot see the sphere, so its center is found mechanically. A sphere resting on three fixed balls always has its center at the same point, whatever direction its stem points. The robot's built-in multi-orientation tool-center-point routine finds the one point on the tool that stays still while the wrist turns, and seating the sphere in the nest from several directions makes that point the sphere's center. Lower the sphere gently for the last millimeter; pressing down bends the stem. The usual causes of a large routine error are a sphere not fully seated or a loose adapter.

slides.title: The board's tool frame sits on its front face
points: Runout: rotate joint 6 through 360 degrees; the dial indicator stays within 0.05 mm
Measure flange-to-face distance D at four places; they agree within 0.05 mm
Tool frame: origin at the face center, z out of the face, x along the long edge
A few degrees of error in x is harmless; an error in z is not
Save as TOOL_BOARD with its load data; record D, the runout and the board size
slides.notes: The board's pose is commanded, not fitted, so its frame must be right. The runout check tests whether the board face is perpendicular to the flange axis; if the reading wanders more than 0.05 mm over a full turn, shim the adapter and repeat. D is the distance from the flange face to the board's front face. Because the board is symmetric, an error of a few degrees in the x direction does no harm, but a tilt of the z axis puts a false slope into every board observation. The board's half-sizes go into the pose log.

slides.title: Four captures locate the sensor well enough to plan

boot.text: About 500 mm in front, near the image center

points: Record the robot's reported TCP position for each
The check tool fits the sphere centers; the plan tool fits the sensor position
Residuals of a few millimeters are fine; tens of millimeters mean a copying error or a wrong TCP
slides.notes: The software determines the sensor's exact position from the full capture set; this step only needs a rough position so that the planned poses land inside the field of view. Four positions not on a line are enough to solve for the sensor's position and orientation. The check tool fits the sphere center in each bootstrap capture, the engineer writes these and the robot positions into boot.json, and the plan tool solves for the sensor and prints the residual of each pair. A residual of tens of millimeters almost always means a position was copied wrongly or the TCP is wrong.

slides.title: The plan spreads 186 poses through the volume

stats.label: sphere A poses at 300, 425 and 550 mm
sphere B poses from 500 to 1,100 mm
board poses at 4 depths, tilted 0, 20 and 40 degrees

slides.caption: About 20 percent of poses are held out to test the fit; they are captured like all the others.
slides.notes: The plan tool writes poses.csv, a summary, and the picture shown here, which plots the planned sphere and board centers in the sensor's frame: a side view on the left and a front view on the right, with the field of view drawn. Sphere A covers the near range on a grid 1.5 radii apart, sphere B the far range, and both appear at 500 to 550 mm. Board poses that would leave the field of view are dropped automatically. A handful of the outermost sphere poses may touch the image border; the check flags them and they are left out of the fit. Poses with a black edge in the picture are the held-out ones.

slides.title: What the robot program must do

columns.head: Inputs
points: poses.csv from the plan tool: base-frame position and orientation of every pose, as a matrix, a quaternion and a rotation vector
Three tool frames: TCP_SPHERE_A_76mm, TCP_SPHERE_B_152mm and TOOL_BOARD

columns.head: Behavior
points: Visit poses in plan order: sphere A, sphere B, board
Pause for each fixture change and activate its tool frame
Same approach every time; settle 1.5 seconds
Never change the base frame during the session

columns.head: Outputs
points: Trigger five frames per pose through the communication software, named <pose_id>_Index00 to _Index04
Append the REPORTED TCP pose to pose_log.csv in the controller's own orientation form; note where the file is written

slides.message: Once the robot model and controller are settled, the robot program can be written with Claude Code.
slides.notes: The robot program is small: it reads the plan, moves, waits, triggers the sensor, and logs what the robot reports. Its interface is fixed by the files on either side: poses.csv from the plan tool on the way in, and the capture file names and pose_log.csv on the way out, whose columns the manifest tool expects. The capture trigger goes through the capture computer's communication software, which already provides it; the program only calls that interface. Note where the program writes pose_log.csv, on the controller or on the network, so it can be collected after the session. Because the input and output formats are already defined, the program can be written with Claude Code as soon as the robot model and its controller are settled; each controller's language and its pose readout differ, which is the part that waits for that choice.

slides.title: Every pose runs the same short robot loop

steps.head: Approach
steps.text: Joint move to 100 mm short along the stem axis, then a linear move onto the pose

steps.head: Settle
steps.text: Wait 1.5 seconds for vibration to die out

steps.head: Log
steps.text: Read the REPORTED TCP pose and append it to the pose log

slides.message: Order: all sphere A poses, then sphere B, then the board. Never move the sensor in between.
slides.notes: The approach is the same every time so that any small hysteresis in the robot is the same for every pose. The settle time lets vibration from the move die out before the sensor captures. The pose that goes in the log is the one the robot reports after it has arrived, not the one it was commanded to; with a robot of 0.1 mm absolute accuracy the difference matters. Remember to activate the right tool frame at each fixture change: TCP_SPHERE_B_152mm for sphere B and TOOL_BOARD for the board.

slides.title: Poses are recorded in the file header or in a pose log

columns.head: Option A: in the file header
points: The capture software writes robotPose, a 4 x 4 matrix, tool to base
No separate log needed beyond the target sizes
Use it if the capture software supports it

columns.head: Option B: pose log and manifest
points: The robot program appends one CSV line per pose
Orientation in the controller's own form: KUKA A, B, C or FANUC W, P, R, quaternion, rotation vector, matrix
make_manifest matches files to poses and names every mismatch
Recommended as a backup even with option A

slides.notes: Both options are supported by the software. In option B the pose log columns are the pose id, the target kind, the radius or the board half-sizes, the reported position, the rotation type and up to four rotation values; the example line is a sphere pose, which needs no rotation. The manifest tool converts every orientation form to a matrix and complains by name about any pose without files, any file without a pose, and any missing size. A pose log is worth keeping even when the headers carry the pose, because it is the only independent record.

slides.title: Check the captures before the robot is put away

cards.head: Low valid fraction
cards.text: Target not read: check exposure, or the target was outside the field

cards.head: Touches the image border
cards.text: Target partly out of view: the pose is unusable; re-plan it slightly inward

cards.head: Sphere center off
cards.text: One pose: position copied wrongly. One sphere: wrong TCP. Growing across the volume: base frame or robot accuracy

cards.head: Board normal off
cards.text: Board tool frame orientation wrong, or the rotation type in the log is misnamed

slides.caption: Re-capture a flagged pose under a new id, for example s038_z0425_017r; never delete lines from the log.
slides.notes: The check tool prints one line per pose and a verdict, and its exit code is 0 when nothing is flagged, 1 when something is, and 2 when it cannot read the manifest. Running it while the fixtures are still mounted means a bad pose can be captured again in minutes instead of setting everything up again another day. The pattern of the sphere-center flags tells you the cause: one pose, one sphere, or a trend across the volume.

slides.title: Two shape checks test the corrected surfaces

columns.head: Sphere shape
points: Each held-out sphere is fitted with its radius free
After correction the fitted radius should match the measured radius
Judge each error against its standard error, which is large for a small or distant sphere

columns.head: Board flatness
points: Each held-out board is fitted with its own plane
After correction the spread should fall toward the plate's flatness
Sees only errors that bend the board; mainly catches the fixed pattern

slides.message: Neither check tests the scale of the volume or a smooth robot error; those rest on the robot's 0.1 mm accuracy.
slides.notes: Nothing in the session has a geometry known independently of the robot, so these two checks use no robot positions at all; the fit's report computes them on the held-out poses, so nothing extra is captured. The technician's part is to make the references good: measure the sphere diameters carefully and keep the board's flatness report. A uniform range-scale error of 0.1 percent changes sphere A's fitted radius by only 0.04 mm, so scale is checked mainly by the held-out sphere centers against the robot.

slides.title: Seven things that spoil a session

items.text: Moving or bumping the sensor: everything after it is a new session
Changing exposure, gain or the base frame mid-session
Logging the commanded pose instead of the reported pose
A loose adapter or a bent stem: roll the stem on a flat surface first
Fingerprints or gloss: wipe the targets with isopropyl alcohol
Letting the stem point toward the sensor: the sphere must hide it
Mixing up the two spheres' radii in the pose log

slides.notes: These are the failures that cannot be repaired afterwards in software. The first two change the sensor itself mid-session, which invalidates the comparison between early and late captures. The third and seventh put wrong numbers into the pose table. The others damage the measurement: a joint that moves shifts the sphere center away from the TCP that was measured, a shiny spot returns a highlight and a bad read, and a visible stem corrupts the sphere fit.

slides.title: What to hand over at the end of the session
checklist: pose_log.csv, or confirmation that the headers carry robotPose
captures/check.json with no flags, or a note on each
plan/ files as used, boot.json and the bootstrap captures
session_notes.txt: sensor serial, warm-up, exposure, gain and SGM parameters, base frame, TCPs, board D and runout, sphere diameters, temperature, pose log location
Photos (a phone camera is fine) of the sensor mount, each fixture on the flange, and the nest

software.head: Software
points: plan_poses, make_manifest and check_captures in sphcal/cli
Install and self-test: procedure appendix C
Every tool prints its options with --help

slides.notes: The checklist is section 10 of the procedure. The session notes matter as much as the data: the fit needs the measured sphere diameters, and the notes are the only record of warm-up time, temperature and fixture changes if a result looks wrong later. The three command-line tools come with the repository; appendix C of the procedure walks through installing Python, creating an environment, installing the package and running the self-test, on Windows or Linux.
